title: Qualys CI Lookup Rules
subtitle: How a scanned host finds its CI

concepts.title: What a CI lookup rule does
bullets: Qualys sends one record per scanned host: DNS name, IP address, operating system, serial number, NetBIOS name. Each record lands as a Discovered Item.
The platform runs the CI lookup rules in order. Each rule reads one source field (serial, DNS or IP) plus the rest of the record, searches the CMDB and returns one CI or nothing.
The first rule that returns a CI wins: the item is matched to it and every vulnerable item of that host attaches to that CI.
When no rule answers, the item stays unmatched and receives a placeholder record (Unclassed Hardware) until it is evaluated again.
Items are evaluated again on the next import, when a rule changes, or on demand with the list action "Reapply CI lookup rules".

concepts.title: Principles the USEM rules share
bullets: Exactly one record or decline. A rule never picks between two candidates; ambiguity stays unmatched for the CMDB to resolve.
The scanned OS sets the class: Red Hat means Linux Server, Windows Server means Windows Server, NetApp means Storage Server. The search stays inside that class first, then goes hardware-wide.
Class agreement: a CI reached through DNS or IP records must be of a class the OS implies (same, parent or child), so a Cisco IOS router never lands on a Computer.
Ignored classes never answer: adapters, IP address records, storage volumes, certificates and the other classes on sn_sec_cmn.ignoreCIClass.
Strongest identifier first: serial, then FQDN, host name with domain, DNS layers, host name, controllers and interfaces, virtual servers, IP address, and a broad name search last.
No fitness heuristics: no "best" record by class depth or last update. A retired duplicate is set aside for the live record; two live records decline.

rules.name: USEM Serial Number Class Match
rules.purpose: A serial number stays with a machine for its whole life, while names and addresses get reused. It is the strongest identifier Qualys gives us, so it is tried first, inside the class the scanned OS points at.
rules.returns: the one CI of that class carrying the serial, else null
rules.before: nothing custom runs before this rule.
rules.after: the hardware-wide serial rule, for hosts whose OS gives no class.

rules.name: USEM Serial Number Hardware Match
rules.purpose: The same serial search across the whole hardware tree. It exists for hosts whose OS gives no usable class, and for CIs that sit in a different class than the OS suggests.
rules.returns: the one hardware CI carrying the serial, else null
rules.before: the class-scoped serial rule already tried the serial inside the OS class.
rules.after: the phone rule and then the name rules.

rules.name: USEM Cisco IP Phone MAC
rules.purpose: Unified Communications Manager names every phone "SEP" followed by its MAC address, and Qualys reports that name as the DNS label. The rule turns the label back into a MAC and finds the one IP Phone CI that carries it.
rules.returns: the one IP Phone CI carrying that MAC, else null
rules.before: the serial rules; phones report no serial.
rules.after: the FQDN and hostname rules, which never see a phone label.
mechanics: Adapter first, then the phone record

rules.name: USEM FQDN Class Match
rules.purpose: The first name rule. An exact FQDN on the CI record is the most precise name evidence there is, so it is matched before any hostname handling, inside the class the OS points at.
rules.reads: DNS, plus the OS and the IP
rules.returns: the one CI of that class whose fqdn equals the scanned name
rules.before: the serial rules and the phone rule found nothing.
rules.after: the hardware-wide FQDN rule, then hostname plus domain.
mechanics: One hit, or the IP breaks the tie

rules.name: USEM FQDN Hardware Match
rules.purpose: The exact FQDN search again, across the whole hardware tree. It picks up the hosts whose OS gives no class and the CIs kept in a generic or different class than the OS suggests.
rules.returns: the one hardware CI whose fqdn equals the scanned name
rules.before: the class-scoped FQDN rule tried the same value inside the OS class.
rules.after: the hostname plus domain rules, for CIs with no fqdn value at all.

rules.name: USEM Hostname Domain Class Match
rules.purpose: For CIs named with the short hostname that carry the domain somewhere else, in dns_domain or in an fqdn that was never copied into the name. Short name and domain are matched together, inside the class the OS points at.
rules.reads: DNS, plus the OS and the IP
rules.returns: the one CI of that class whose domain evidence agrees
rules.before: the FQDN rules looked in the fqdn field and found nothing.
rules.after: the hardware-wide variant, the layered DNS rule, then the plain hostname rules.
mechanics: One confirmed CI, IP as tie-break

rules.name: USEM Hostname Domain Hardware Match
rules.purpose: Short hostname plus domain evidence again, across the whole hardware tree, for CIs classed generically (Server, Computer) or differently from the scanned OS.
rules.returns: the one hardware CI whose domain evidence agrees
rules.before: the class-scoped variant tried the same evidence inside the OS class.
rules.after: the layered DNS rule and then the plain hostname rules.

rules.name: USEM Layered DNS Match
rules.purpose: Discovery keeps names and addresses as their own records linked to the device. This rule follows that chain, the only way to find a host whose name is not written on the CI record at all, and it resolves aliases to the real machine.
rules.returns: the CI at the end of DNS Name to IP Address to adapter to CI
rules.before: the FQDN and hostname-plus-domain rules read fields on the CI record.
rules.after: the plain hostname rules and the full-FQDN name rule.
mechanics: Follow the chain in one query
Count owners, note the IP path
One CI, or the IP decides

rules.name: USEM Hostname Class Match
rules.purpose: The short hostname alone, inside the class the scanned OS points at. For CIs that carry only a short name and no domain information; the agreement between CI class and scanned OS stands in for the missing domain evidence.
rules.returns: the one CI of that class named with the short hostname
rules.before: every rule so far needed domain evidence on the CI.
rules.after: the hardware-wide short name rule with a class sanity check.

rules.name: USEM Hostname Hardware Match
rules.purpose: The short hostname across the whole hardware tree, with a check that the CI found does not contradict the scanned OS. For CIs classed generically (Server, Computer, UNIX Server) or differently from the OS.
rules.returns: the one hardware CI named with the hostname, class permitting
rules.before: the class-scoped rule required the name to be unique inside the OS class.
rules.after: the full-FQDN name rule, then the address rules.

rules.name: USEM Device Name Match
rules.purpose: IP Phones and Scanners sit outside the Hardware tree, so the hardware-wide name rules never see them, and they report no OS. This rule looks for the scanned host name in exactly those two classes.
rules.reads: DNS, plus the OS and the IP
rules.returns: the one IP Phone or Imaging Hardware CI named with the host name; the scanned address breaks a tie
rules.before: USEM Hostname Hardware Match, which searches the Hardware tree only.
rules.after: USEM Management Interface Match.
mechanics: Refuse when the OS names a server or desktop
Host name searched in IP Phone and Imaging Hardware
One device, else the scanned address breaks the tie

rules.name: USEM Management Interface Match
rules.purpose: Server management controllers (HP iLO, Oracle ILOM, Dell iDRAC, IBM IMM, Cisco CIMC, BMC, IPMI) are scanned under their own label, the server name plus a suffix. The findings belong to the server, so the rule strips the suffix and matches the server.
rules.returns: the one hardware CI named like the label without its suffix
rules.before: the hostname rules tried the whole label and found nothing.
rules.after: the network interface rule and the full-FQDN name rule.
mechanics: Two ways to recognise a controller

rules.name: USEM Network Interface Name Match
rules.purpose: Network devices are scanned through their interface and VLAN addresses, each carrying a label of the device name plus an interface tail. The device CI is named with the leading part only, so the rule walks the label prefix by prefix.
rules.returns: the one Network Gear or Load Balancer device named by a prefix
rules.before: the hostname rules tried the whole label; the controller rule found no suffix.
rules.after: the full-FQDN name rule and the load balancer service rule.

rules.name: USEM FQDN Name Hardware Match
rules.purpose: Some loads name the CI with the whole FQDN string instead of the short hostname, typically the appliance domains ending in .rpg, so a short name search can never find them.
rules.returns: the one hardware CI whose name is exactly the scanned FQDN
rules.before: every rule so far compared the short hostname or the fqdn field.
rules.after: the address rules, and finally the broad name rule.

rules.name: USEM Load Balancer Member Match
rules.purpose: Many virtual servers front exactly one real server. When the CMDB holds the pool behind the virtual server and every member leads to one and the same machine, the findings belong to that machine.
rules.reads: IP, plus the OS and the DNS name
rules.returns: the one real server behind the virtual server; null with several machines, a member the CMDB cannot place, or no pool data
rules.before: the hardware rules, which decline a virtual address.
rules.after: USEM Load Balancer Service Match, which attaches the virtual server record when the CMDB does not show several servers behind it.
mechanics: VIP sign: load balancer OS or a VIP marker in the name
Virtual server found on fqdn, then name, then address
Service to Pool to Pool Member to server
One machine behind the whole pool, else decline

rules.name: USEM Load Balancer Service Match
rules.purpose: A virtual IP answered by a load balancer is not the balancer, and the hardware rules refuse the balancer device on purpose. Such hosts belong to the Load Balancer Service CI that models the VIP.
rules.reads: IP, plus the OS and the DNS name
rules.returns: the one Load Balancer Service CI for that VIP
rules.before: the hardware rules declined: no serial, no server name, address on a balancer.
rules.after: the ordinary address rules, for hosts that are not VIPs.

rules.name: USEM IP Class Match
rules.purpose: The first address rule. An address is the least trustworthy identifier: addresses move between machines and are shared by load balancers. It is used only for hosts with no serial and no usable name, inside the class the OS points at.
rules.returns: the one CI of that class whose ip_address equals the scanned address
rules.before: every serial and name rule; a host with no DNS name makes them all decline.
rules.after: the hardware-wide address rule, then the adapter and layered rules.

rules.name: USEM IP Hardware Match
rules.purpose: The address across the whole hardware tree, with two extra safety checks: the CI must not be a load balancer, and its class must not contradict the scanned OS.
rules.returns: the one hardware CI on that address, balancer and class permitting
rules.before: the class-scoped address rule required a CI of the OS class.
rules.after: the adapter rule and the layered address rule.

rules.name: USEM IP Adapter Match
rules.purpose: Discovery stores one Network Adapter record per network card, and a multi-homed server keeps its addresses there rather than on the CI record. This rule finds the adapter carrying the address and takes its owning CI.
rules.returns: the CI that owns the adapter carrying the scanned address
rules.before: the address rules so far read the ip_address field of the CI record.
rules.after: the layered address rule and then the broad name rule.

rules.name: USEM IP Layered Match
rules.purpose: Newer discovery writes each address as its own IP Address record linked to the adapter, and the adapter record itself may carry no address. This rule reads those records, two links from the CI.
rules.returns: the CI at the end of IP Address to adapter to CI
rules.before: the adapter rule looked for the address on the adapter records.
rules.after: the broad name rule, and after that the out-of-box Qualys rules.
mechanics: One owner, and not a balancer

rules.name: USEM FQDN Name Broad Match
rules.purpose: The one deliberately late, broad fallback: a CI named with the full FQDN anywhere in the CI table, classes outside the hardware tree included, such as a virtual machine instance.
rules.returns: the one CI in any class named exactly with the scanned FQDN
rules.before: every hardware-scoped rule has declined for this host.
rules.after: the out-of-box Qualys rules: host id, cloud resource id, FQDN, NetBIOS, DNS.
mechanics: Root CI table, exactly one CI
